title: Systems, row reduction, span, solution sets
summary: How to solve any linear system by row reduction and read off existence and uniqueness from pivots. The link "A x = b consistent ⇔ b ∈ span of the columns" and the structure "particular + homogeneous" underlie every later unit.

lesson.title: Linear systems and their three possible outcomes

blocks.text: An equation a₁x₁ + a₂x₂ + ⋯ + aₙxₙ = b with numbers a₁, …, aₙ, b. No products of variables, no powers, no functions of variables.
A list (s₁, …, sₙ) that makes every equation true at once. The solution set is the set of all solutions. Two systems are equivalent if they have the same solution set.

blocks.name: Three outcomes
blocks.text: A linear system has either no solution, exactly one solution, or infinitely many solutions. A system with at least one solution is consistent; with none, inconsistent.

proof.text: Why never exactly two: if x and y are different solutions, then every point x + t(y − x) on the line through them is also a solution (plug in: the equations are linear), so there are infinitely many.

blocks.text: We store a system as its augmented matrix: the coefficients, then a bar, then the right-hand sides. The system x₁ − 2x₂ = −1, −x₁ + 3x₂ = 3 becomes
(1) Replacement: add a multiple of one row to another. (2) Interchange: swap two rows. (3) Scaling: multiply a row by a nonzero constant.

Each row operation is reversible, and it never changes the solution set: anything that solves the old equations solves the new ones and vice versa. That is why we may row reduce freely and read the answer from the simplest matrix.

lesson.title: Echelon form, RREF, pivots, free variables

blocks.text: (1) All zero rows are at the bottom. (2) Each leading entry (first nonzero entry of a row) is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above. (3) Entries below a leading entry are zero.
Echelon form, plus: every leading entry is 1, and it is the only nonzero entry in its column.

blocks.name: Uniqueness of the RREF
blocks.text: Each matrix is row equivalent to exactly one reduced echelon matrix. (Echelon forms are not unique, but the pivot positions are.)
A pivot position is the location of a leading 1 in the RREF of A. A pivot column is a column containing a pivot position.
Variables matching pivot columns are basic; the rest are free (they can be any number, and the basic variables are solved in terms of them).

blocks.title: Row reduction algorithm
items: Forward phase: take the leftmost nonzero column; swap a nonzero entry to the top; use replacements to create zeros below it.
Cover that row and repeat on the submatrix below until you reach echelon form.
Backward phase: starting from the rightmost pivot, scale each pivot to 1 and create zeros above it.
Read off: pivot columns ↔ basic variables; other columns ↔ free variables.

blocks.title: Row reduce and name pivots and free variables
blocks.prompt: Row reduce the augmented matrix [1 2 −1 3 | 4; 2 4 0 2 | 6; −1 −2 3 −7 | −6] to RREF. Name the pivot columns and free variables.
steps: R₃ − R₂ → [0 0 0 0 | 0]. Echelon form reached: pivots in columns 1 and 3.
Scale R₂ by ½ → [0 0 1 −2 | −1]. Then R₁ + R₂ → [1 2 0 1 | 3].
Pivot columns 1 and 3 ⇒ x₁, x₃ basic; x₂, x₄ free.
blocks.answer: Pivots in columns 1, 3; free variables x₂, x₄; no row 0 = nonzero, so consistent with infinitely many solutions.

blocks.text: Free variables are decided by the coefficient columns only. The augmented column is never a 'free variable', and a pivot in the augmented column means inconsistency, not a solution.

lesson.title: Existence and uniqueness from the echelon form

blocks.name: Existence and Uniqueness Theorem
blocks.text: A system is consistent iff the rightmost (augmented) column is not a pivot column, i.e. no echelon row looks like [0 ⋯ 0 | c] with c ≠ 0. If consistent, the solution is unique when there are no free variables and there are infinitely many when there is at least one free variable.

A row [0 ⋯ 0 | c] says 0 = c. Everything else can be solved by back-substitution, with free variables as parameters. Each free variable adds one direction of solutions, so even one free variable gives infinitely many.

blocks.title: Decide consistency
blocks.prompt: Is the system with augmented matrix [1 2 −1 3 | 4; 2 4 0 2 | 6; −1 −2 3 −7 | −8] consistent?
steps: That row says 0 = −2: the augmented column is a pivot column.

blocks.text: Counting pivots answers most questions without solving. For an m×n coefficient matrix there are at most min(m, n) pivots, and #free variables = n − #pivots.

blocks.title: Why a 3×5 system is never unique
blocks.prompt: Can a system of 3 equations in 5 unknowns have exactly one solution?
steps: Each pivot uses its own row, so there are at most 3 pivots.
5 columns − at most 3 pivots ⇒ at least 2 free variables.
If the system is consistent, the free variables give infinitely many solutions; otherwise none.
blocks.answer: No: it has either no solution or infinitely many.

blocks.title: Parameter problem
blocks.prompt: For which h, k does x₁ + hx₂ = 2, 4x₁ + 8x₂ = k have no solution, exactly one, infinitely many?
steps: Augmented matrix [1 h | 2; 4 8 | k]. R₂ − 4R₁ → [0 8 − 4h | k − 8].
If 8 − 4h ≠ 0 (h ≠ 2): two pivots, no free variable ⇒ exactly one solution, whatever k is.
If h = 2: the row is [0 0 | k − 8]. If k ≠ 8 it says 0 = nonzero ⇒ no solution.
If h = 2 and k = 8: the row is all zeros, x₂ is free ⇒ infinitely many.
blocks.answer: Unique iff h ≠ 2; none iff h = 2, k ≠ 8; infinitely many iff h = 2, k = 8.

blocks.text: A parameter in the coefficient part decides whether a pivot is lost; a parameter in the augmented column decides whether the lost row reads 0 = 0 or 0 = nonzero. You need both to classify.
An ordered list of n real numbers written as a column. Add entrywise, scale entrywise. Geometrically an arrow from the origin (or a point).
y = c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₚvₚ with scalars (weights) c₁, …, cₚ.

Span{v₁, …, vₚ} = the set of all linear combinations of v₁, …, vₚ. It always contains 0 (all weights 0). In ℝ³: span of one nonzero vector is a line through 0; of two non-parallel vectors, a plane through 0.

blocks.name: Vector equation = augmented matrix
blocks.text: x₁a₁ + ⋯ + xₙaₙ = b has the same solution set as the system with augmented matrix [a₁ ⋯ aₙ | b]. So b is in Span{a₁, …, aₙ} iff that system is consistent.

proof.text: Comparing the vector equation entry by entry gives exactly the rows of the system: row i says x₁(a₁)ᵢ + ⋯ + xₙ(aₙ)ᵢ = bᵢ.

blocks.title: Is b in the span?
steps: Consistent with x₁ = 1, x₂ = 1, so b = v₁ + v₂. Check: (1+2, 0+1, −2−3) = (3, 1, −5). ✓
For (3, 1, −4) the same steps end with [0 0 | 1]: 0 = 1.
blocks.answer: (3, 1, −5) = v₁ + v₂ is in the span; (3, 1, −4) is not.

lesson.title: The matrix equation Ax = b and spanning ℝᵐ

blocks.text: If A = [a₁ ⋯ aₙ] is m×n and x ∈ ℝⁿ, then Ax = x₁a₁ + ⋯ + xₙaₙ, a vector in ℝᵐ. (Row–vector rule: entry i of Ax is row i of A dotted with x.)

blocks.name: Three views of one problem
blocks.text: Ax = b, the vector equation x₁a₁ + ⋯ + xₙaₙ = b, and the system [A | b] all have the same solutions. Hence Ax = b is consistent exactly when b is a linear combination of the columns of A, i.e. b ∈ Span{columns}.

proof.text: Ax is by definition a combination of the columns with weights x₁, …, xₙ. Asking for some x with Ax = b is asking for weights that build b from the columns.

blocks.name: Spanning theorem (Lay Thm 4)
blocks.text: For an m×n matrix A, these are all true or all false: (a) Ax = b has a solution for every b ∈ ℝᵐ; (b) every b is a combination of the columns; (c) the columns span ℝᵐ; (d) A has a pivot position in every row.

proof.text: If some row of an echelon form U of A has no pivot, it is a zero row. Choose a right side making that row read 0 = 1 and undo the row operations: you get a b with Ax = b inconsistent. If every row has a pivot, no row can read 0 = c ≠ 0, so every system is consistent.

blocks.text: The test is a pivot in every row of the coefficient matrix A, not of [A | b]. And n vectors in ℝᵐ with n < m can never span ℝᵐ (at most n pivots for m rows).

blocks.title: Do the columns span ℝ³? Which b work?
blocks.prompt: Let A = [1 3 4; −4 2 −6; −3 −2 −7]. Is Ax = b consistent for all b? If not, describe the b that work.
steps: Row reduce [A | b]: R₂ + 4R₁ → [0 14 10 | 4b₁ + b₂]; R₃ + 3R₁ → [0 7 5 | 3b₁ + b₃].
R₃ − ½R₂ → [0 0 0 | b₁ − ½b₂ + b₃].
Only 2 pivots for 3 rows ⇒ the columns do not span ℝ³.
Consistent exactly when b₁ − ½b₂ + b₃ = 0, i.e. 2b₁ − b₂ + 2b₃ = 0: a plane through 0.
blocks.answer: No. Ax = b is consistent iff 2b₁ − b₂ + 2b₃ = 0 (Col A is that plane).

lesson.title: Solution sets: homogeneous systems and parametric vector form

blocks.text: Ax = 0. It always has the trivial solution x = 0. It has a nontrivial solution iff there is at least one free variable.
Writing the solution set as x = p + su + tv + ⋯ with free variables s, t, … as parameters.

blocks.name: Structure of solution sets
blocks.text: If Ax = b is consistent and p is any one solution, the solution set is exactly {p + vₕ : Avₕ = 0}, i.e. p + (solutions of the homogeneous system).

proof.text: If Avₕ = 0 then A(p + vₕ) = b + 0 = b. Conversely if Aw = b, then A(w − p) = 0, so w = p + (a homogeneous solution).

blocks.text: Geometrically: the homogeneous solutions form a line/plane through 0; the nonhomogeneous ones form the parallel line/plane shifted by p. So uniqueness for one b means the homogeneous system has only the trivial solution, which forces at most one solution for every b.

blocks.title: Writing parametric vector form
items: Row reduce [A | b] to RREF.
Write each basic variable in terms of the free variables.
Write x as a column, substitute, and split it into a constant vector plus one vector per free variable.
Check: A(constant vector) = b, A(each direction vector) = 0.

blocks.title: Parametric vector form
blocks.prompt: Write the solution set of the system [1 2 −1 3 | 4; 2 4 0 2 | 6; −1 −2 3 −7 | −6] in parametric vector form, and its homogeneous version.
steps: From the RREF [1 2 0 1 | 3; 0 0 1 −2 | −1; 0 0 0 0 | 0]: x₁ = 3 − 2x₂ − x₄, x₃ = −1 + 2x₄, with x₂, x₄ free.
The homogeneous system has solution set Span{(−2, 1, 0, 0), (−1, 0, 2, 1)}: drop p.

blocks.text: If b ≠ 0, the solution set is not a span (it does not contain 0); it is a translated span.

lesson.title: True/False reasoning on existence and uniqueness

blocks.text: A true statement needs a reason that works for every matrix; a false one needs one concrete counterexample. The tools are: the existence/uniqueness theorem, the pivot-in-every-row theorem, pivot counting (≤ min(m, n) pivots), and the structure theorem p + Nul.

blocks.title: Four quick True/False
blocks.prompt: (a) If A is 3×5, Ax = 0 has a nontrivial solution. (b) If A is 5×3, Ax = b is consistent for every b. (c) If Ax = b has a free variable, it has infinitely many solutions. (d) If [A | b] has a pivot in every row, the system is consistent.
steps: (a) True: at most 3 pivots, 5 columns ⇒ ≥ 2 free variables, and the homogeneous system is always consistent.
(b) False: at most 3 pivots for 5 rows ⇒ some row has no pivot ⇒ the columns cannot span ℝ⁵.
(c) False as stated: the system might be inconsistent (a free variable plus a row 0 = 1, e.g. [1 1 | 0; 0 0 | 1]). True if it is consistent.
(d) False: [1 1 | 0; 0 0 | 1] has a pivot in every row, but one is in the augmented column.
blocks.answer: (a) T (b) F (c) F (true only if consistent) (d) F

blocks.text: 'Consistent' and 'unique' are separate questions: consistency is about the augmented column (or rows of A), uniqueness is about free variables (columns of A).

cards.front: When is a linear system consistent? (Existence and Uniqueness Theorem)

back.text: Consistent iff the augmented column is not a pivot column (no echelon row [0 ⋯ 0 | c], c ≠ 0). Then: unique if no free variables, infinitely many if at least one.

cards.front: What are the three elementary row operations, and why don't they change solutions?

back.text: Replacement (add a multiple of a row to another), interchange, scaling by a nonzero constant. Each is reversible, so the old and new systems imply each other.

cards.front: Echelon form vs reduced echelon form?

back.text: REF: zero rows at bottom, leading entries step right, zeros below leading entries. RREF additionally: leading entries are 1 and are the only nonzero entries in their columns. RREF is unique; REF is not, but pivot positions are.

cards.front: Basic vs free variables?

back.text: Basic: variables of pivot columns. Free: all others; they are parameters and the basic variables are expressed in terms of them.

cards.front: Why can a linear system never have exactly two solutions?

back.text: If x ≠ y are solutions, every x + t(y − x) is a solution (linearity), so there are infinitely many.

cards.front: A x = b is consistent exactly when…?

back.text: b is a linear combination of the columns of A, i.e. b ∈ Span{a₁, …, aₙ}. Reason: A x = x₁a₁ + ⋯ + xₙaₙ by definition.

cards.front: Four equivalent statements of the spanning theorem for m×n A?

back.text: A x = b solvable for every b ⇔ every b is a combination of the columns ⇔ columns span ℝᵐ ⇔ pivot in every row of A.

cards.front: Why can a 3×5 system never have a unique solution?

back.text: At most 3 pivots (one per row) but 5 columns ⇒ at least 2 free variables. So: no solution or infinitely many.

cards.front: Can 3 vectors span ℝ⁴?

back.text: No. The 4×3 matrix has at most 3 pivots, so some row has no pivot.

cards.front: What is Span{v₁, …, vₚ}? Does it contain 0?

back.text: All linear combinations c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₚvₚ. Yes, always (all weights 0). In ℝ³: a point, line or plane through 0, or all of ℝ³.

cards.front: How do you test whether b ∈ Span{v₁, …, vₚ}?

back.text: Row reduce [v₁ ⋯ vₚ | b]. In the span iff consistent; the solution gives the weights.

cards.front: When does A x = 0 have a nontrivial solution?

back.text: Iff there is at least one free variable (fewer pivots than columns). Always true when n > m.

cards.front: Structure of the solution set of A x = b (consistent)?

back.text: x = p + vₕ, where p is one particular solution and vₕ ranges over all solutions of A x = 0.
If b ≠ 0 it is not a span: it misses 0.

cards.front: Parametric vector form recipe?

back.text: RREF → basic variables in terms of free ones → split x into constant vector + (free variable)·(vector) for each free variable. Check A p = b, A v = 0.

cards.front: Pivot in every row of [A | b]: consistent?

back.text: Not necessarily. A pivot in the augmented column means 0 = 1. The spanning test uses the coefficient matrix A.

cards.front: If A x = b has a unique solution for one b, what about other c?

back.text: At most one solution for every c (Nul A = {0}), but possibly none. E.g. A = [1; 0].

cards.front: How do you handle a parameter problem (for which h, k)?

back.text: Row reduce symbolically. A coefficient that might vanish decides whether a pivot is lost; then the right side of the lost row decides 0 = 0 (infinite) vs 0 = nonzero (none).

cards.front: Row–vector rule for A x?

back.text: Entry i of A x is (row i of A)·x. Column view: A x = x₁a₁ + ⋯ + xₙaₙ.

cards.front: Find all b making A x = b consistent: method?

back.text: Row reduce [A | b] with b₁, b₂, b₃ symbolic. Each zero row of A's echelon form gives a linear condition on b that must equal 0.

cards.front: Polynomial span question: is q in Span{p₁, p₂, p₃} ⊂ ℙ₂?

back.text: Write each polynomial as its coefficient vector in {1, t, t²} and row reduce [p₁ p₂ p₃ | q]. Watch for dependent generators: three polynomials need not span ℙ₂.

cards.front: Homogeneous solution set geometry vs nonhomogeneous?

back.text: Homogeneous: a span (line/plane through 0). Nonhomogeneous: the same line/plane translated by p.

hard.title: Two-parameter classification

prompt.text: Consider the system with augmented matrix
(a) For which h, k does it have no solution, exactly one, infinitely many? (b) In the infinite case, write the solution set in parametric vector form.

hard.answer: h ≠ 3: exactly one; h = 3, k ≠ 8: none; h = 3, k = 8: infinitely many, x = (−1, 2, 0) + z(3, −2, 1)

solution.title: Solution
items: h ≠ 3: three pivots in the coefficient part ⇒ exactly one solution (any k).
h = 3, k ≠ 8: last row reads 0 = 8 − k ≠ 0 ⇒ no solution.
h = 3, k = 8: z free ⇒ infinitely many. Back-substitute: y = 2 − 2z, x = 3 − 2y − z = −1 + 3z.

solution.text: What it tests: Classifying needs both parameters: h decides whether a pivot is lost, k decides whether the lost row is 0 = 0 or 0 = nonzero. Students who answer “h = 3 ⇒ infinitely many” lose half the points.

hard.title: Span with a parameter

prompt.text: Let v₁ = (1, −1, 2), v₂ = (2, 1, h), v₃ = (0, 3, 4). For which h is Span{v₁, v₂, v₃} ≠ ℝ³? For that h, describe the span by a single linear equation and write v₃ as a combination of v₁, v₂.

hard.answer: h = 8; span is the plane 10x + 4y − 3z = 0; v₃ = −2v₁ + v₂

solution.text: Three vectors span ℝ³ ⇔ [v₁ v₂ v₃] has 3 pivots ⇔ its determinant ≠ 0 (or row reduce).
det
= 1(4 − 3h) − 2(−4 − 6) + 0 = 24 − 3h = −3(h − 8). So the span fails to be ℝ³ exactly when h = 8.
The span is the plane through 0 with normal v₁ × v₂ = (−10, −4, 3), i.e. 10x + 4y − 3z = 0. (Row-reducing [v₁ v₂ | b] gives the same condition.)
What it tests: Span = ℝ³ is a pivot-in-every-row question. The plane equation is the consistency condition on b; get it from the zero row of the reduced [A | b] if you don’t like cross products.

items: 1. If Ax = b is consistent for some b, then Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution.
2. A 3×5 matrix A has Ax = b consistent for every b in ℝ³ if and only if A has 3 pivot positions.
3. If the augmented matrix [A | b] has a pivot in every row, the system is consistent.
4. If x₁ and x₂ both solve Ax = b, then x₁ − x₂ solves Ax = 0.
5. If b ≠ 0, the solution set of Ax = b can be written as Span{v₁, …, vₖ} for suitable vectors.

solution.text: 1. False. Take A =
and b = 0. The system is consistent, yet (1, −1) is a nontrivial solution of Ax = 0. Consistency says nothing about free variables.
2. True. Consistent for every b ⇔ columns span ℝ³ ⇔ a pivot in every row of A (the coefficient matrix). 3 rows, so 3 pivots.
3. False.
has a pivot in each row, but the second pivot is in the augmented column: 0 = 1. The test is a pivot in every row of A, not of [A | b].
5. False. Every span contains 0, but A0 = 0 ≠ b. The solution set is a translate p + Span{…}, never a span itself.
What it tests: A true statement needs a reason valid for every matrix; a false one needs one concrete counterexample. “Pivot in every row” always refers to the coefficient matrix.

hard.title: Construct a matrix with given column space

prompt.text: Construct a 3×3 matrix A with no zero entries such that Ax = b is consistent exactly when b₁ − 2b₂ + b₃ = 0. Justify.

hard.answer: e.g. A = [1 1 2; 1 2 3; 1 3 4] (columns span the plane b₁ − 2b₂ + b₃ = 0)

solution.text: Consistent ⇔ b ∈ Col A. So we need Col A = the plane b₁ − 2b₂ + b₃ = 0 (a 2-dimensional subspace).
Pick columns in that plane, two of them independent: (1, 1, 1), (1, 2, 3), and their sum (2, 3, 4). Each satisfies b₁ − 2b₂ + b₃ = 0.
. Columns 1, 2 are independent and column 3 = col 1 + col 2, so Col A is exactly the plane (2-dimensional subspace of a 2-dimensional plane).
Check by row reduction: [A | b] → last row [0 0 0 | b₁ − 2b₂ + b₃]. ✓

What it tests: Both directions matter: columns in the plane gives “consistent ⇒ condition”; columns spanning the plane gives “condition ⇒ consistent”. Three multiples of one vector would fail the second.

hard.title: Proof: one unique solution ⇒ at most one always

prompt.text: Let A be m×n. Prove: if Ax = b has exactly one solution for some particular b, then Ax = c has at most one solution for every c.

hard.answer: Uniqueness for one b ⇒ A x = 0 has only x = 0 ⇒ at most one solution for every c (possibly none)

solution.text: Let p be the unique solution of Ax = b. If Au = 0, then A(p + u) = b, so p + u = p by uniqueness, i.e. u = 0. Hence Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution.
Now suppose Ay₁ = Ay₂ = c. Then A(y₁ − y₂) = 0, so y₁ − y₂ = 0. At most one solution. ∎
(It can have zero solutions: A =
has a unique solution for b = (1, 0) and none for (0, 1).)
What it tests: The structure theorem: every solution set of Ax = b is either empty or p + Nul A. Uniqueness anywhere ⇔ Nul A = {0}. Don’t claim “exactly one for every c”.

hard.title: Reverse-engineer A from its solution set

prompt.text: The general solution of Ax = b, where A is 3×4, is x = (1, 2, 0, 0) + s(1, −1, 1, 0) + t(0, 2, 0, 1), with s, t free.
(a) How many pivot columns does A have? (b) Do the columns of A span ℝ³? (c) Find one such A and b.

solution.text: (a) Two free parameters ⇒ 2 free variables ⇒ 4 − 2 = 2 pivot columns.
(b) Only 2 pivots among 3 rows ⇒ some row has no pivot ⇒ columns do not span ℝ³.
Take A =
(third row = sum, so rank 2 and Nul A is exactly the 2-D span). Then b = A(1, 2, 0, 0) = (1, 3, 4).

What it tests: Free parameters = n − (number of pivots). Rows of A must be orthogonal to the homogeneous directions; then b = Ap. Forgetting to keep rank exactly 2 (e.g. three independent rows) changes the solution set.

hard.title: Span in ℙ₂ with parameters
hard.answer: q is in the span iff h − k = 3

solution.text: Use coordinates in the basis {1, t, t²}: the spanning vectors become (1, 2, 1), (2, 3, 1), (1, 1, 0) and q becomes (3, h, k).
Notice (1, 1, 0) = (2, 3, 1) − (1, 2, 1): the third polynomial is redundant, so the span is 2-dimensional.
Row reduce
In the span ⇔ h − k = 3. E.g. 3 + 5t + 2t² is in it; 3 + 4t + 2t² is not.

What it tests: Polynomial span questions are column-vector span questions in disguise. With three generators in a 3-D space, it’s tempting to say “three vectors, so they span” — check dependence first.

hard.title: Consistency without knowing A

prompt.text: A is 4×4. Ax = e₁, Ax = e₂, Ax = e₃ are each consistent, but Ax = e₄ is not.
(a) What is Col A? (b) How many solutions does Ax = 0 have? (c) How many solutions does Ax = 2e₁ − e₃ have? (d) Is Ax = e₂ + e₄ consistent?

hard.answer: (a) Span{e₁, e₂, e₃} (b) infinitely many (c) infinitely many (d) inconsistent

solution.title: Solution
items: (a) Col A is a subspace containing e₁, e₂, e₃, so it contains Span{e₁, e₂, e₃}, which is 3-dimensional. It is not all of ℝ⁴ (misses e₄). So Col A = Span{e₁, e₂, e₃} = {x₄ = 0}.
(b) rank 3 ⇒ one free variable ⇒ infinitely many solutions.
(c) 2e₁ − e₃ ∈ Col A (consistent) and there is a free variable ⇒ infinitely many.
(d) If Ax = e₂ + e₄ had a solution x, and Ay = e₂, then A(x − y) = e₄, contradiction. Inconsistent.

solution.text: What it tests: Col A is closed under combinations — that’s what makes the problem solvable without knowing A. For a square matrix, failing to be onto forces failing to be one-to-one (IMT preview).

keyFacts: Consistent ⇔ no echelon row [0 ⋯ 0 | c] with c ≠ 0 (augmented column is not a pivot column).
Consistent + no free variables ⇒ unique; consistent + a free variable ⇒ infinitely many.
A x = b consistent ⇔ b ∈ Span{columns of A}, because A x = x₁a₁ + ⋯ + xₙaₙ.
Columns span ℝᵐ ⇔ A x = b solvable for all b ⇔ pivot in every ROW of A.
A x = 0 has a nontrivial solution ⇔ a free variable exists (always if n > m).
Solution set of consistent A x = b is p + {solutions of A x = 0}; never a span if b ≠ 0.
More columns than rows: never a unique solution. More rows than columns: never consistent for every b.
